# Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array

**Binary Search** · medium · [the same question on LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array/)

> Everything about this problem is on this page: the question, what the input
> promises, the hints, the long explanation, every approach in Python, Java and C++,
> and a script you can run. It **does not hide anything** — if you are partway
> through the journey for this problem, it will show you the ending.

A sorted array of distinct values was rotated at an unknown pivot (e.g. [4,5,6,1,2,3]). Return its minimum element in O(log n).

## What the input promises

- 1 <= nums.length <= 5000
- -5000 <= nums[i] <= 5000
- every value is distinct
- nums is a sorted array rotated between 1 and n times — a rotation of n leaves it sorted

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `nums = [4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3]` | `1` | — |
| `nums = [1, 2, 3]` | `1` | Rotation by zero is allowed. |

<details>
<summary>Hints, one nudge at a time — open them in order</summary>

1. The array is two sorted runs; the minimum starts the second run.
2. Compare nums[mid] with nums[hi]: which side of the break are you on?
3. nums[mid] > nums[hi] → break (and minimum) is right of mid. Otherwise mid could itself be the minimum — keep it in range.

</details>

---

## Understanding the Problem

Someone took a sorted list of distinct numbers, cut it at one unknown point, and swapped the two
pieces. `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]` cut between `6` and `1` and swapped arrives as `[4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3]`.
Find the smallest value, and do it in `O(log n)`.

Say what you are looking at, because the name "rotated" hides it: the array is **two ascending runs
laid end to end**, and every value in the first run is larger than every value in the second. There
is exactly one place where the order breaks — call it the **seam** — and the minimum is the first
element of the second run, sitting immediately after that seam.

**The core question:** where is the seam? Not "what is the smallest value" — you already know the
smallest value is whatever sits just right of the break. The naive approach is slow because it reads
every element to find a thing that only a handful of probes are needed to *locate*: it treats the
array as an unordered bag when it is very nearly sorted.

> **Intuition.** Picture a dial — a combination lock face — with the numbers written around it in
> order. Rotating the dial does not change the order of the numbers, it only changes where you
> start reading. So there is still exactly one step in the whole circle where the number goes
> *down* instead of up, and the minimum is on the low side of that step. Everything below is the
> search for that one step.

### The constraints, and what each one unlocks

| Constraint | What it means for you |
|---|---|
| `1 <= nums.length <= 5000` | Small. `O(n)` would pass comfortably in practice, so the `O(log n)` requirement is **stated in the problem**, not forced by the input size — this is a problem that grades the *method*, not the wall clock. Also: the array is never empty, so `nums[0]` always exists and `lo <= hi` holds at entry. |
| `-5000 <= nums[i] <= 5000` | Values straddle zero, so **no constant is a safe seed** for a running extremum in either direction — initialise from an actual element. (Approach 1 runs the `best = 0` bug and shows that the usual "it breaks on negatives" warning has the direction backwards.) |
| every value is **distinct** | **This is the constraint the whole logarithmic solution rests on.** Because no two elements are equal, a probe compared against an end is either strictly greater or strictly less — never ambiguous — so one comparison always eliminates half the array. Remove this promise and the `O(log n)` guarantee collapses; the last section of this document does exactly that and shows the damage. |
| rotated between 1 and n times — a rotation of `n` leaves it **sorted** | The un-rotated array `[1, 2, 3]` is legal input. Any formulation that assumes a seam actually exists inside the range needs an extra branch to survive it. **The right-end formulation does not, and that is precisely why it is the one to memorise.** |

The worked example used in every section below is the statement's own:

```
nums = [4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3]        answer: 1
```

The seam is between index 2 (`6`) and index 3 (`1`). The first run is `[4, 5, 6]`, the second is
`[1, 2, 3]`, and `1` starts the second run.

---

## Approach 1 — Read everything and keep the smallest

### The idea

*How do I find the minimum of a list?* Look at every element and remember the smallest one seen.
This is the answer you would give if nobody had told you the array was sorted-then-rotated, and it
is worth writing down precisely so you can see what it fails to use: **it never compares two
elements of the array to each other, only each element to a running best.** All the structure in
the input is thrown away.

### How to think about it

> **Intuition.** You are walking down a row of numbered doors with a notepad, writing down the
> smallest number you have seen so far and crossing it out whenever you see a smaller one. It
> works on *any* row of doors — shuffled, sorted, rotated, it makes no difference. That universality
> is exactly the problem. A method that cannot tell a sorted row from a shuffled one cannot be
> faster on the sorted one, and "faster on the sorted one" is the entire assignment here.

### Worked example

`nums = [4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3]`.

| step | index | `nums[index]` | smaller than best? | best after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 4 | — (first) | 4 |
| 1 | 1 | 5 | no | 4 |
| 2 | 2 | 6 | no | 4 |
| 3 | **3** | **1** | **yes** | **1** |
| 4 | 4 | 2 | no | 1 |
| 5 | 5 | 3 | no | 1 |

Six reads to learn one fact. Notice rows 4 and 5: by the time you reach them you are re-confirming
something the *structure* already guaranteed — everything after the seam ascends, so nothing past
index 3 could possibly beat index 3.

### Code

```python
def rotated_min_linear_scan(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    return min(nums)
```

### Common mistake

> **Watch out.** The misconception is that a "starting value" for a running minimum is free
> bookkeeping. It is a **claim that the answer is at most that value** — and `0` makes that claim
> without any evidence from the data.

Hand-rolling the scan with `best = 0` instead of `best = nums[0]`:

```python
    best = 0                        # WRONG: a sentinel, not an element
    for x in nums:
        best = min(best, x)
```

On the worked example this returns **0** instead of 1 — and `0` does not appear in the array at all,
which is the giveaway that a sentinel rather than an element is being reported.

Now the part that is worth running rather than reasoning about, because the folklore version of this
warning is *"it breaks on negative arrays"* and that is **backwards**. On `[-2, -1, -5, -4, -3]` the
buggy version returns **−5**, the correct answer: every element is below the sentinel, so the
sentinel never wins. The bug fires when the true minimum is **positive**, and stays invisible on
exactly the negative inputs people write the test for. The real rule has nothing to do with signs:
a running extremum must be seeded from the data, because any constant you choose is an unproven
claim about the answer. Python's `min()` cannot get this wrong — it is initialised from the data by
construction — which is the real reason to use it.

### Complexity and when to use this

**Time** `O(n)`, **space** `O(1)`. The time is one read per element with a constant comparison each; the
space is the single running best. There is no way to do better *without* using the sortedness,
which is the point being made.

Use it when the input genuinely has no order to exploit, and use it here as the **oracle** in a test
harness — it is the version whose correctness you can see by reading it, which is what you need to
cross-check the clever ones. In an interview, say it in one sentence, name the `O(n)`, and say the
problem has explicitly asked for better.

---

## Approach 2 — Find the seam by walking

### The idea

*The array is two ascending runs — can I just look for the join?* Yes. Walk left to right comparing
each element to its neighbour. Exactly one adjacent pair goes **down** instead of up, and the
smaller half of that pair is the answer. If no pair ever goes down, the array was not rotated and
the minimum is at the front.

This fixes Approach 1's weakness — **it never compares two array elements to each other, so it
learns nothing about the array's shape.** This one names the shape: *seam*. It is still linear, but
it is linear for a reason you can now attack.

### How to think about it

> **Intuition.** Read the row out loud going up — "four, five, six, **one**" — and the moment your
> voice goes down instead of up, stop; you just stepped over the seam. What makes this rung
> worth writing even though it is no faster is that it converts the question from "what is the
> smallest value" into "where is the one descending step", and *where* questions are the ones
> binary search can answer. You cannot binary-search for a minimum directly, but you can
> binary-search for a boundary.

### Worked example

`nums = [4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3]`.

| `i` | `nums[i]` | `nums[i+1]` | descends? | action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 4 | 5 | no | continue |
| 1 | 5 | 6 | no | continue |
| **2** | **6** | **1** | **yes** | return `nums[3]` = **1** |
| 3 | — | — | — | never reached |

Three comparisons here, but that is luck of the draw: rotate the same array so the seam sits at the
end — `[2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1]` — and the walk makes all five comparisons before it finds anything. The
worst case is what the cost is, and the worst case is `n − 1`.

### Code

```python
def rotated_min_find_the_drop(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    for i in range(len(nums) - 1):
        if nums[i] > nums[i + 1]:
            return nums[i + 1]  # the seam: everything after here ascends from this value
    return nums[0]  # no descent anywhere, so the array was never rotated
```

### Common mistake

> **Watch out.** The misconception is that the loop's fallthrough is defensive padding. It is not —
> it is the **only** path taken on an un-rotated array, which the constraints explicitly permit
> ("a rotation of n leaves it sorted"). Deleting it, or returning the wrong thing from it, breaks a
> legal input class rather than a rare one.

Returning `nums[i]` instead of `nums[i + 1]` at the seam:

```python
        if nums[i] > nums[i + 1]:
            return nums[i]      # WRONG — that is the LARGEST value, not the smallest
```

On the worked example this returns **6** instead of 1. The two sit either side of the same break, so
the bug is a single character and the symptom is the maximum rather than the minimum — which,
usefully, is loud. The half-formed wrong idea underneath it is "I found the interesting index, so I
return the interesting index"; the seam is a *gap between two positions*, and you have to say which
side of the gap you want.

### Complexity and when to use this

**Time** `O(n)`, **space** `O(1)`. The cost is `n − 1` comparisons in the worst case — when the seam is at
the far end, or absent. Space is a loop counter.

No faster than Approach 1, and in Python it is slower, since `min()` runs in C. Use this rung purely
as thinking: it is the sentence "the answer is the element just past the one descending step" that
the next two approaches accelerate. If you are actually shipping a linear solution, ship `min()`.

---

## Approach 3 — Binary search against the *left* end *(an addition — not in the data file)*

### The idea

*If the seam is a boundary, can binary search find it?* It can — a probe at `mid` need only answer
"am I before the seam or after it", and comparing `nums[mid]` against the array's **first** element
answers exactly that. Anything `>= nums[0]` is in the first run, so the seam is strictly to the
right; anything smaller is in the second run, so the seam is at `mid` or left of it.

This fixes Approach 2's weakness — **it inspects every adjacent pair to locate one boundary**, and
gets to `O(log n)`. It also drags in a wart, which is the reason Approach 4 exists.

### How to think about it

> **Intuition.** Hold up the first element as a **yardstick**. Every element of the first run is at
> least as big as the yardstick; every element of the second run is smaller than it. So one glance
> at any probe tells you which run you landed in, and therefore which direction the seam lies.
> The yardstick is the trick, and the yardstick is also the flaw: an un-rotated array has *no*
> second run, every element is at least the yardstick, and the search happily walks off the right
> end reporting the largest value. You have to notice that case before the loop starts, not inside
> it.

> **Why it works.** The invariant is that the minimum's index always lies inside `[lo, hi]`. When
> `nums[mid] >= nums[0]`, `mid` is in the first run, and **the first run cannot contain the
> minimum** — every element of it is at least `nums[0]`, while in a genuinely rotated array the
> minimum is strictly less than `nums[0]` — so discarding `[lo, mid]` discards nothing that could
> be the answer. When `nums[mid] < nums[0]`, `mid` is in the second run and is itself a candidate,
> so it is kept and only `(mid, hi]` is discarded: the second run ascends, so everything right of
> `mid` inside it is strictly larger. The range shrinks every iteration because `lo = mid + 1`
> moves past `mid`, and `hi = mid` is a strict decrease whenever `lo < hi`.

### Worked example

`nums = [4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3]`. The guard first: is `nums[0] <= nums[-1]`, i.e. `4 <= 3`? No, so the
array really is rotated and the loop is safe to enter. The yardstick is `nums[0] = 4` throughout —
**fixed**, never re-read as `lo` moves.

| iter | `lo` | `hi` | `mid` | `nums[mid]` | `>= 4`? | which run | new `lo`, `hi` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 5 | 2 | 6 | yes | first | `lo = 3`, `hi = 5` |
| 2 | 3 | 5 | 4 | 2 | no | second | `lo = 3`, `hi = 4` |
| 3 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 1 | no | second | `lo = 3`, `hi = 3` |
| — | 3 | 3 | — | — | — | range closed | answer `nums[3]` = **1** |

Three probes against Approach 2's three comparisons — a tie on this input, and a rout on a large
one: at `n = 5000` this is 13 probes against up to 4999.

### Code

```python
def rotated_min_binary_left_anchor(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    if nums[0] <= nums[-1]:  # not rotated: no second run exists for the loop to find
        return nums[0]
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    first = nums[0]  # the yardstick is FIXED; nums[lo] moves and would lie
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] >= first:
            lo = mid + 1  # mid is in the first run, which cannot hold the minimum
        else:
            hi = mid  # mid is in the second run and may itself be the minimum
    return nums[lo]
```

### Common mistake

> **Watch out.** The misconception is that `nums[lo]` and `nums[0]` are the same yardstick, because
> `lo` starts at `0`. They diverge the first time `lo` moves, and after that the comparison is
> measuring the probe against a member of the run it is already inside — which is no information
> at all.

Reading the yardstick live as `nums[lo]`:

```python
        if nums[mid] >= nums[lo]:   # WRONG — nums[lo] is not nums[0] after the first move
            lo = mid + 1
```

On the worked example this returns **3** instead of 1. Trace why: after iteration 1, `lo = 3`, so the
yardstick silently becomes `nums[3] = 1`; the next probe at `mid = 4` finds `2 >= 1` and concludes
"first run", pushing `lo` to 5 — past the minimum it was standing next to. The number it reports,
`3`, is the last element of the array, and nothing about it looks like a sentinel or a crash. **This
is the most common way this problem is failed**, and the cure is to hoist the yardstick into a named
variable before the loop, where it cannot be accidentally re-read.

The second way it fails is deleting the guard. Without the `nums[0] <= nums[-1]` line, the sorted
input `[1, 2, 3]` returns **3** — every element is `>= nums[0]`, so `lo` marches to the last index.
The constraints allow that input explicitly, so this is not a corner case, it is a whole legal
input class.

### Complexity and when to use this

**Time** `O(log n)`, **space** `O(1)`. The range halves every iteration and each iteration does a fixed
amount of work, so the probe count is `⌈log₂ n⌉` — 13 at `n = 5000`. Space is three integers.

This is the version most people write first, and it is correct **once the guard is there**. Use it
if the left-end comparison is the one you find easier to reason about — but know that you are
carrying a special case the next rung does not need, and special cases are where re-derivation under
pressure goes wrong.

## Approach 4 — Binary search against the *right* end

### The idea

*Can the special case be designed away rather than guarded against?* Yes — compare `nums[mid]`
against `nums[hi]` instead of `nums[0]`. If `nums[mid] > nums[hi]`, the probe is in the first run and
the seam is strictly right of it. Otherwise the probe is in the second run — or the window is
already entirely ascending — and either way the minimum is `mid` or left of it.

This fixes Approach 3's weakness — **an un-rotated array has no second run, so the fixed-left
yardstick needs a guard before the loop.** Against the right end, an un-rotated array simply takes
the "otherwise" branch every time and walks `hi` down onto index 0, which is the correct answer with
no branch written for it.

### How to think about it

> **Intuition.** Instead of measuring each probe against the *front* of the row, measure it against
> the *back*. That one swap changes the question from "which run am I in, given that two runs
> exist" to "does the window still ascend from me to its last element" — a question that has a
> sensible answer whether or not the array was ever rotated. That is the difference between the
> two formulations, and it is not stylistic: one of them has a case to remember and one of them
> does not.

> **Why it works.** Two claims, one per branch, and each says what the discarded half **cannot**
> contain.
>
> *If `nums[mid] > nums[hi]`:* the values do not ascend from `mid` to `hi`, so the seam lies
> strictly between them. `mid` is therefore in the first run, and so is every index from `lo` to
> `mid` — the window ascends from `lo` up to the seam. **`nums[lo..mid]` cannot contain the
> minimum**, because the minimum is the element immediately right of the seam and the seam is right
> of `mid`. Discard it: `lo = mid + 1`.
>
> *Otherwise (`nums[mid] < nums[hi]`; with distinct values there is no third case):* the window
> `nums[mid..hi]` ascends without a break, so **`nums[mid+1..hi]` cannot contain the minimum** —
> every one of those elements is strictly greater than `nums[mid]`. Discard them but keep `mid`,
> which is still a candidate: `hi = mid`.
>
> The loop ends when `lo == hi`, and the invariant "the minimum's index is in `[lo, hi]`" was
> preserved by both branches, so that one surviving index is it. Termination: `lo = mid + 1`
> strictly raises `lo`, and `hi = mid` strictly lowers `hi` whenever `lo < hi`, because
> `mid = (lo + hi) // 2 < hi` in that case.

### Worked example

`nums = [4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3]`. No guard, no yardstick variable — the anchor is whatever `nums[hi]`
currently is, and it moves with the window.

| iter | `lo` | `hi` | `mid` | `nums[mid]` | `nums[hi]` | `nums[mid] > nums[hi]`? | new `lo`, `hi` | window |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 5 | 2 | 6 | 3 | **yes** — seam is right of `mid` | `lo = 3`, `hi = 5` | `[1, 2, 3]` |
| 2 | 3 | 5 | 4 | 2 | 3 | no — `[2, 3]` ascends | `lo = 3`, `hi = 4` | `[1, 2]` |
| 3 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 1 | 2 | no — `[1, 2]` ascends | `lo = 3`, `hi = 3` | `[1]` |
| — | 3 | 3 | — | — | — | range closed | — | answer `nums[3]` = **1** |

And the case that motivated the whole approach, on `nums = [1, 2, 3]` — same code, no special case:

| iter | `lo` | `hi` | `mid` | `nums[mid]` | `nums[hi]` | greater? | new `lo`, `hi` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 2 | 1 | 2 | 3 | no | `lo = 0`, `hi = 1` |
| 2 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 2 | no | `lo = 0`, `hi = 0` |
| — | 0 | 0 | — | — | — | closed | answer `nums[0]` = **1** |

`hi` simply walks down to the front. That is the guard Approach 3 had to write, arriving for free.

### Code

```python
def rotated_min_binary_right_anchor(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] > nums[hi]:
            lo = mid + 1  # nums[lo..mid] is the first run: all of it exceeds the minimum
        else:
            hi = mid  # nums[mid..hi] ascends, so nothing right of mid can be the minimum
    return nums[lo]
```

Four lines of body and no special case. Compare it to Approach 3 side by side — same shape, one
fewer thing to remember — and that is the entire argument for preferring it.

### Common mistake

> **Watch out.** The misconception is that `hi = mid` is a timid version of `hi = mid - 1` and the
> tighter one must be at least as good. They are not variants: `hi = mid - 1` **throws away the
> only candidate the branch just identified.** The branch's whole conclusion was "`mid` might be
> the answer".

Tightening the else branch:

```python
        else:
            hi = mid - 1      # WRONG — discards mid, which this branch just called a candidate
```

On the worked example this returns **1** — the correct answer. That is what makes it dangerous: the
bug is invisible on the input you are most likely to test with. Run it on `nums = [3, 1, 2]` and it
returns **3** instead of 1: the first probe at `mid = 1` finds `nums[1] = 1 <= nums[2] = 2`, sets
`hi = 0`, the loop exits with `lo = 0`, and the answer reported is the largest element in the array.

A related claim that turns out **not** to be a bug, and is worth stating so you do not go hunting
for it: writing `>=` instead of `>` in the comparison. With distinct values `mid < hi` always holds
inside the loop, so `nums[mid]` and `nums[hi]` are never equal and the two operators are
indistinguishable — checked over every rotation of every distinct array up to `n = 10`, **zero
differences**. It stops being harmless the moment duplicates are allowed, and the next section is
where that matters.

### Complexity and when to use this

**Time** `O(log n)`, **space** `O(1)`. Each iteration halves the window and does two integer comparisons,
so the probe count is `⌈log₂ n⌉`: 13 at the constraint's `n = 5000`, against up to 4999 for either
linear rung. Space is two integers and a midpoint.

**This is the one to write.** It is the shortest correct formulation, it has no input class that
needs remembering, and the same probe-against-an-end reasoning is what runs the rotated-*search*
problem next door. The assumption it needs is the one the constraints hand you — **values are
distinct**. The next section removes that assumption and shows exactly what it costs.

---

## Approach 5 — When the values are **not** distinct *(an addition — the standard follow-up)*

### The idea

*What happens if the promise of distinctness is withdrawn?* The comparison stops being decisive.
`nums[mid] == nums[hi]` tells you nothing about which side of the seam you are on, so there is no
half you can safely discard — only one element you can safely give up. The repair is a third branch
that shrinks `hi` by exactly one, and the price is a linear worst case.

This does not fix a weakness in Approach 4; it **relaxes an assumption** Approach 4 depends on, and
it is the follow-up you will be asked for. Most write-ups skip it, which is why it is worth
over-learning.

### How to think about it

> **Intuition.** The probe and the right end hold the same value — say both are `3`, in
> `[3, 3, 1, 3, 3]` and in `[3, 3, 3, 3, 3]`. In the first, the minimum is to the probe's right; in
> the second there is nothing to find and any index will do. **The two situations are
> indistinguishable from the two values you are holding**, so any rule that discards a half is
> guessing, and on one of the two arrays it guesses wrong. What you *can* say is narrower and still
> true: since `nums[hi]` equals `nums[mid]`, which is still inside the window, throwing away `hi`
> alone cannot lose the answer — if `nums[hi]` was the minimum, an equal copy of it remains in
> range at `mid`.

> **Why it works.** The two strict branches are unchanged and still discard halves that provably
> cannot hold the minimum, exactly as argued in Approach 4. The new branch discards a **single**
> index, and it is safe because `nums[mid] == nums[hi]` with `lo <= mid < hi` means the value at
> `hi` is duplicated at `mid`, which stays inside the window. So the invariant survives — note its
> weakening from "*the* index of the minimum is in `[lo, hi]`" to "*an* index holding the minimum
> value is in `[lo, hi]`", which is the honest statement once duplicates exist.

### Worked example

On the document's array `nums = [4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3]` this is line-for-line Approach 4 — no two
elements are equal, so the third branch never fires and the trace is the same three rows. The
section earns its keep on an array the other approaches were never promised:

`nums = [3, 3, 1, 3, 3]`, a rotation of `[1, 3, 3, 3, 3]`. Answer `1`.

| iter | `lo` | `hi` | `mid` | `nums[mid]` | `nums[hi]` | branch | new `lo`, `hi` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 4 | 2 | 1 | 3 | less → `hi = mid` | `lo = 0`, `hi = 2` |
| 2 | 0 | 2 | 1 | 3 | 1 | greater → `lo = mid + 1` | `lo = 2`, `hi = 2` |
| — | 2 | 2 | — | — | — | closed | answer `nums[2]` = **1** |

Two probes, because the duplicates happened not to line up. Now the case that kills it —
`nums = [3, 3, 3, 3, 3]`: every probe finds `nums[mid] == nums[hi]`, every iteration retires exactly
one index, and the loop runs `n − 1` times. Measured on 5000 identical values: **4999 iterations**,
against 13 for a distinct array of the same length.

### Code

```python
def rotated_min_with_duplicates(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] > nums[hi]:
            lo = mid + 1
        elif nums[mid] < nums[hi]:
            hi = mid
        else:
            hi -= 1  # ambiguous: give up ONE index, the only safe move
    return nums[lo]
```

### Common mistake

> **Watch out.** The misconception is that duplicates are a detail the existing comparison
> absorbs — that folding the tie into one of the two branches with `>=` or `<=` is "close enough".
> A tie is not a small version of a greater-than; it is the **absence** of information, and a
> branch that acts on it is acting on nothing.

Folding the tie into the discard-the-left branch — `if nums[mid] >= nums[hi]: lo = mid + 1` — is the
usual form of the guess. Over the 20 000 random rotated arrays drawn from the values `0..3` that this
document's script generates, that version reports the wrong minimum **1388 times**. The equally
tempting other fold, keeping plain `>` so ties land in `hi = mid`, is wrong **132 times** over the
same 20 000 — fewer, and therefore *more* dangerous, because it will pass a small test suite. Both
guesses lose; only the one-index retreat is sound, and it is right on all 50 000 duplicate-laden
cases in the stress test.

The mitigation, when you control the input rather than the algorithm: **de-duplicate the ends before
searching.** Once, up front, walk `hi` down while `nums[hi] == nums[lo]`; the loop is then
information-rich again for as long as the array is not mostly one repeated value. It does not remove
the `O(n)` worst case — nothing can, because an array of `n − 1` copies of one value hiding a single
smaller one forces any correct algorithm to inspect almost everything — it only makes the common
case fast again.

### Complexity and when to use this

**Time** `O(log n)` average, **`O(n)` worst case**; **space** `O(1)`. The cost split is the whole lesson:
the two strict branches halve the window, and the tie branch retires one index. An input with few
ties is indistinguishable from Approach 4; an input of all-equal values degrades to a scan with
extra steps. The worst case is not an implementation artefact — it is **information-theoretic**. With
`n − 1` equal values hiding one smaller one anywhere, no algorithm can rule out a position it has
not read.

Use it whenever distinctness is not promised, and say the worst case out loud when you do. In an
interview this is almost always the follow-up to Approach 4, and the strongest answer names the
`O(n)` *and* explains that it is unavoidable rather than a flaw in the implementation.

---

## The Overall Arc

The single principle every rung chases is **make one probe eliminate a half**, and what makes that
possible is a reframing that happens before any code: the array is not a bag of numbers, it is two
ascending runs joined at one seam, and the minimum is not a value to be found but a *boundary* to be
located. Approach 1 declines the reframing entirely — `min()` compares every element to a running
best and never compares two elements to each other, so it cannot be faster on an almost-sorted array
than on a shuffled one, and reading all `n` is the price of that indifference. Approach 2 accepts the
reframing and finds the seam honestly, comparing every adjacent pair until one descends; it is no
faster, but it converts the question into a *where* question, and *where* questions are the ones
binary search answers. From there the only remaining design decision is what a probe should be
compared against, and the two choices are not equal. Measuring `nums[mid]` against the fixed front
element works, but only behind a guard for the un-rotated array, whose second run does not exist —
and that guard is the kind of thing that evaporates under pressure, right alongside the subtler trap
of re-reading the yardstick as `nums[lo]` after `lo` has moved. Measuring against the moving right
end asks a question with a sensible answer in both worlds: either the window ascends cleanly to its
last element, in which case nothing right of the probe can be the minimum, or it does not, in which
case the seam is right of the probe and nothing left of it can be. Two branches, no special case,
and each branch justified by naming what the discarded half **cannot** contain — which is the
sentence to be able to say, because it is what distinguishes having derived binary search from
having memorised it. The last rung then removes the assumption everything above quietly leans on:
distinctness is what makes a comparison against an end *decisive*, and withdrawing it turns
`nums[mid] == nums[hi]` into the absence of information rather than a third case to be clever about,
so no half can be discarded and the honest repair gives up a single index at a time for an `O(n)`
worst case that no algorithm can avoid. Read everything, find the seam by walking, halve against the
front with a guard, halve against the back without one — and then know precisely which promise the
last of those was spending.

---

## Comparison

| Approach | Time | Space | Core trade-off | Best used when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Linear scan (`min`) | `O(n)` | `O(1)` | Uses no structure at all, so it is immune to every subtlety below — and to every speed-up | The oracle in a test harness; input with no promised order |
| Find the drop | `O(n)` | `O(1)` | Same cost, but names the seam — the reframing the fast versions need | Teaching, and as the sentence you say before writing the binary search |
| Binary search, left anchor | `O(log n)` | `O(1)` | Logarithmic, at the price of a guard for the un-rotated array and a yardstick that must not be re-read | You find "which run am I in" the more natural question — and you remember the guard |
| **Binary search, right anchor** | **`O(log n)`** | **`O(1)`** | **No special case at all; needs distinct values to stay decisive** | **The default answer, and the shape to carry into rotated-search** |
| Duplicate-tolerant | `O(log n)` avg, `O(n)` worst | `O(1)` | Gives up one index when the comparison says nothing, trading the guarantee for correctness | Values are not promised distinct — the standard follow-up |

---

## Interview Priority

> **In an interview.** Say the reframing before you write anything: *"this is two ascending runs
> with one seam, and the minimum is the first element after the seam — so I am searching for a
> boundary, not a value."* Then write the right-anchor version and justify each branch by what it
> **rules out**: "if `nums[mid] > nums[hi]` the seam is right of `mid`, so the minimum cannot be in
> `nums[lo..mid]`." The follow-up is **always** duplicates. Answer it in two parts — the comparison
> stops being decisive, so you retreat one index instead of discarding a half; and the worst case
> becomes `O(n)` and *cannot* be better, because `n − 1` equal values hiding one smaller one force
> any algorithm to read almost everything.

**Memorize cold — the right-anchor binary search (Approach 4).** Five lines, no special case, and it
is the version you can reconstruct from the invariant rather than from memory: `hi = mid` keeps the
candidate, `lo = mid + 1` discards a run that cannot contain the answer. Practise it until the
`hi = mid` versus `hi = mid - 1` choice is automatic, because that is the one that silently returns
the right answer on `[4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3]` and the wrong one on `[3, 1, 2]`.

**Memorize cold — the duplicate story.** Not code: two sentences. Equal values destroy the ability to
tell which half is ordered; the only safe move is to retire one index, giving an `O(n)` worst case,
which is optimal because the information is genuinely absent. A candidate who volunteers this before
being asked is signalling that they derived the algorithm rather than recalled it.

**Worth understanding, not memorizing — the left-anchor version (Approach 3).** Know it exists, know
why it needs the guard, and above all know the `nums[lo]`-instead-of-`nums[0]` trap, because you will
meet that bug in other people's code and in your own under time pressure. Do not choose it for the
whiteboard; choosing the formulation with fewer cases is itself part of what is being assessed.

**Not worth memorizing — the two linear rungs.** But say them. Name `min()` as the one-line baseline,
name the seam walk as the idea the binary search accelerates, reject both on the stated `O(log n)`
requirement, and move on inside thirty seconds. Naming the baseline and killing it on a stated
constraint is the part interviewers score.

## The same ladder, in Python, Java and C++

The explanation above works in Python. This is the app's own ladder for this
problem — the approaches it teaches, in build order — with every rung in all
three languages. Where the two differ, the explanation above may carry extra
rungs; each is labelled where it appears.


---

## Rung 1 — Linear scan

Take the minimum of the array. Correct, one line, and exactly what the problem forbids you to settle for — it reads every element because it assumes nothing, which is the right instinct on unstructured data and the wrong one here. Naming it is how you find out what structure is left to exploit once the array has been rotated.

```python
def rotated_min(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    return min(nums)
```

**O(n) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int rotatedMin(int[] nums) {
    int min = nums[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < nums.length; i++) {
        if (nums[i] < min) min = nums[i];
    }
    return min;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
int rotatedMin(const vector<int>& nums) {
    int minVal = nums[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < (int)nums.size(); i++) {
        if (nums[i] < minVal) minVal = nums[i];
    }
    return minVal;
}
```

</details>

---

## Rung 2 — Find the drop

> **Why now.** min() reads everything and learns nothing about the array. Looking for the one place where the order breaks names the structure - the seam - even though it still walks the whole thing.

Scan for the single place where a value is larger than the one after it: the rotation seam, which is also the minimum. Still linear, and it earns its rung by naming the structure the binary search will use — a rotated sorted array has exactly ONE descent, so finding it is a search for a local property rather than a comparison of every element.

```python
def rotated_min(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    for i in range(len(nums) - 1):
        if nums[i] > nums[i + 1]:
            return nums[i + 1]
    return nums[0]  # not rotated
```

**O(n) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int rotatedMin(int[] nums) {
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length - 1; i++) {
        if (nums[i] > nums[i + 1]) return nums[i + 1];
    }
    return nums[0];
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
int rotatedMin(const vector<int>& nums) {
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)nums.size() - 1; i++) {
        if (nums[i] > nums[i + 1]) return nums[i + 1];
    }
    return nums[0];
}
```

</details>

---

## Rung 3 — The one to remember

> **Why now.** Naming the seam is not the same as finding it quickly. Comparing the middle against the right end says which half the seam is in, so the search halves at every step.

Binary search on the break point. If nums[mid] > nums[hi], the middle sits in the first (larger) run, so the minimum lies strictly right: lo = mid + 1. Otherwise mid is in the second run — the minimum is mid or left of it: hi = mid. Loop until the range closes; comparing against nums[hi] rather than nums[lo] avoids ambiguity when the rotation is zero.

```python
def rotated_min(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] > nums[hi]:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return nums[lo]
```

**O(log n) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int rotatedMin(int[] nums) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = nums.length - 1;
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
        if (nums[mid] > nums[hi]) {
            lo = mid + 1;
        } else {
            hi = mid;
        }
    }
    return nums[lo];
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
int rotatedMin(const vector<int>& nums) {
    int lo = 0;
    int hi = (int)nums.size() - 1;
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
        if (nums[mid] > nums[hi]) {
            lo = mid + 1;
        } else {
            hi = mid;
        }
    }
    return nums[lo];
}
```

</details>

---

## The arc

The narrative version is **The Overall Arc**, above. In one line:

> The array is not sorted, yet binary search still applies, and understanding why is the point: a probe can always tell which HALF is ordered by comparing the middle to an end, and the minimum must lie in the half that is not.

| # | Approach | Cost | What it adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Linear scan | O(n) time · O(1) space | the baseline — nothing before it |
| 2 | Find the drop | O(n) time · O(1) space | min() reads everything and learns nothing about the array. Looking for the one place where the order breaks names the structure - the seam - even though it still walks the whole thing. |
| 3 | The one to remember | O(log n) time · O(1) space | Naming the seam is not the same as finding it quickly. Comparing the middle against the right end says which half the seam is in, so the search halves at every step. |

## Full Runnable Script

Every approach above, plus a test suite covering the statement's two examples, the smallest legal
input, both two-element cases, seams at either extreme, all-negative and zero-spanning arrays, the
`hi = mid - 1` trap case, every rotation of three small arrays, and 400 randomised distinct cases —
all cross-checked against `min()`. The duplicate-tolerant approach is then checked separately on
50 000 random arrays **with** duplicates, where the other four are not promised to work, alongside
the two folded-tie variants whose failure counts are quoted in Approach 5, and the probe count on
5000 identical values that Approach 5 quotes as 4999.

```python
"""Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array - every approach in one file, plus a self-checking test suite.

Run: python rotated_min_all.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import random

# --- 1. Read everything and keep the smallest ---------------------------------

def rotated_min_linear_scan(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    return min(nums)

# --- 2. Find the seam by walking ----------------------------------------------

def rotated_min_find_the_drop(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    for i in range(len(nums) - 1):
        if nums[i] > nums[i + 1]:
            return nums[i + 1]  # the seam: everything after here ascends from this value
    return nums[0]  # no descent anywhere, so the array was never rotated

# --- 3. Binary search against the LEFT end (needs a guard) --------------------

def rotated_min_binary_left_anchor(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    if nums[0] <= nums[-1]:  # not rotated: no second run exists for the loop to find
        return nums[0]
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    first = nums[0]  # the yardstick is FIXED; nums[lo] moves and would lie
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] >= first:
            lo = mid + 1  # mid is in the first run, which cannot hold the minimum
        else:
            hi = mid  # mid is in the second run and may itself be the minimum
    return nums[lo]

# --- 4. Binary search against the RIGHT end (optimal, no special case) --------

def rotated_min_binary_right_anchor(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] > nums[hi]:
            lo = mid + 1  # nums[lo..mid] is the first run: all of it exceeds the minimum
        else:
            hi = mid  # nums[mid..hi] ascends, so nothing right of mid can be the minimum
    return nums[lo]

# --- 5. Duplicate-tolerant (O(n) worst case, and that is unavoidable) ---------

def rotated_min_with_duplicates(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] > nums[hi]:
            lo = mid + 1
        elif nums[mid] < nums[hi]:
            hi = mid
        else:
            hi -= 1  # ambiguous: give up ONE index, the only safe move
    return nums[lo]

APPROACHES = [
    ("linear_scan", rotated_min_linear_scan),
    ("find_the_drop", rotated_min_find_the_drop),
    ("binary_left_anchor", rotated_min_binary_left_anchor),
    ("binary_right_anchor", rotated_min_binary_right_anchor),
    ("with_duplicates", rotated_min_with_duplicates),
]

# --- the buggy variants, kept ONLY so the document's quoted numbers stay honest

def _bug_zero_seeded_min(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    best = 0  # WRONG: a sentinel, not an element, on an array that may be all negative
    for x in nums:
        best = min(best, x)
    return best

def _bug_moving_yardstick(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    if nums[0] <= nums[-1]:
        return nums[0]
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] >= nums[lo]:  # WRONG: nums[lo] is not nums[0] after the first move
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return nums[lo]

def _bug_no_guard(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] >= nums[0]:  # WRONG without the un-rotated guard
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return nums[lo]

def _bug_hi_mid_minus_one(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] > nums[hi]:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1  # WRONG: discards the candidate this branch just identified
    return nums[lo]

def _fold_tie_discard_left(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] >= nums[hi]:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return nums[lo]

def _fold_tie_keep_left(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] > nums[hi]:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return nums[lo]

def rotations(values: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
    """Scaffolding, not an answer: every rotation of a sorted list."""
    s = sorted(values)
    return [s[r:] + s[:r] for r in range(len(s))]

def main() -> None:
    cases: list[tuple[str, list[int]]] = [
        ("statement example", [4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3]),
        ("rotation by zero", [1, 2, 3]),
        ("smallest legal input", [7]),
        ("two elements, rotated", [2, 1]),
        ("two elements, not rotated", [1, 2]),
        ("seam at the very end", [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1]),
        ("seam right after the front", [6, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]),
        ("all negative", [-2, -1, -5, -4, -3]),
        ("spans zero", [3, 4, -5000, -1, 0, 2]),
        ("the hi = mid - 1 trap", [3, 1, 2]),
    ]
    for base in ([1, 2, 3, 4], [10, 20, 30, 40, 50], [-3, -1, 0, 4, 9, 11, 12]):
        for arr in rotations(base):
            cases.append((f"every rotation of {base}", arr))

    rng = random.Random(20260912)
    for _ in range(400):
        n = rng.randint(1, 40)
        base = rng.sample(range(-5000, 5001), n)
        cases.append((f"stress distinct n={n}", rng.choice(rotations(base))))

    width = max(len(name) for name, _ in APPROACHES)
    all_agreed = True
    shown = 0

    for label, nums in cases:
        verbose = shown < 10
        if verbose:
            shown += 1
            print(f"\n{label}: nums={nums}")
        results = []
        for name, fn in APPROACHES:
            got = fn(list(nums))
            results.append(got)
            if verbose:
                print(f"  {name:<{width}} -> {got}")
        if any(r != results[0] for r in results) or results[0] != min(nums):
            all_agreed = False
            print(f"  DISAGREEMENT on {label}: {nums} -> {results}")

    print(f"\n{len(cases)} distinct-value cases, {len(APPROACHES)} approaches, all cross-checked against min().")

    # --- the numbers the document quotes, re-measured ---------------------------
    print("\nquoted numbers, re-measured:")
    print(f"  best = 0 seed on [4,5,6,1,2,3]         -> {_bug_zero_seeded_min([4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3])}  (document says 0)")
    print(f"  best = 0 seed on [-2,-1,-5,-4,-3]      -> {_bug_zero_seeded_min([-2, -1, -5, -4, -3])}  (document says -5: NOT a bug on negatives)")
    print(f"  moving yardstick on [4,5,6,1,2,3]      -> {_bug_moving_yardstick([4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3])}  (document says 3)")
    print(f"  no un-rotated guard on [1,2,3]         -> {_bug_no_guard([1, 2, 3])}  (document says 3)")
    print(f"  hi = mid - 1 on [4,5,6,1,2,3]          -> {_bug_hi_mid_minus_one([4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3])}  (document says 1, i.e. invisible)")
    print(f"  hi = mid - 1 on [3,1,2]                -> {_bug_hi_mid_minus_one([3, 1, 2])}  (document says 3)")

    ge_differs = 0
    for n in range(1, 11):
        for arr in rotations(list(range(n))):
            a, b = rotated_min_binary_right_anchor(arr), _fold_tie_discard_left(arr)
            if a != b:
                ge_differs += 1
    print(f"  '>=' vs '>' over every distinct rotation to n=10 -> {ge_differs} differences  (document says 0)")

    # --- duplicates: only approaches 1, 2 and 5 are promised to work here ------
    dup_bad = 0
    fold_left_bad = fold_right_bad = 0
    seen = 0
    for _ in range(50_000):
        n = rng.randint(1, 12)
        base = sorted(rng.randint(0, 3) for _ in range(n))
        arr = rng.choice(rotations(base))
        want = min(arr)
        if rotated_min_with_duplicates(list(arr)) != want:
            dup_bad += 1
        if seen < 20_000:
            seen += 1
            if _fold_tie_discard_left(list(arr)) != want:
                fold_left_bad += 1
            if _fold_tie_keep_left(list(arr)) != want:
                fold_right_bad += 1

    identical = [7] * 5000
    lo, hi, probes = 0, 4999, 0
    while lo < hi:  # the tie branch's cost on the worst input there is
        probes += 1
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if identical[mid] > identical[hi]:
            lo = mid + 1
        elif identical[mid] < identical[hi]:
            hi = mid
        else:
            hi -= 1

    print("\nduplicates, 50000 random rotations of values drawn from 0..3:")
    print(f"  with_duplicates wrong                    {dup_bad} times")
    print(f"  tie folded into 'discard left' (>=)      {fold_left_bad} times of the first 20000  (document says 1388)")
    print(f"  tie folded into 'keep left'   (>)        {fold_right_bad} times of the first 20000  (document says 132)")
    print(f"  probes on 5000 identical values:         {probes}  (document says 4999; a distinct array takes 13)")
    if dup_bad:
        all_agreed = False

    print(
        "\nALL APPROACHES AGREED ON EVERY CASE."
        if all_agreed
        else "\nMISMATCH: the approaches did NOT all agree."
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```
